title: The burning bush (Exodus 3:1–6)
hookLine: a bush on fire and not burned up: take off your shoes, this is holy ground
last: A STRANGER IN A STRANGE LAND.

cards: Years pass, in process of time, as the King James text says. The king of Egypt dies, the Israelites groan under their slavery and cry out, and God hears. Moses doesn't know any of that.

He's a shepherd now, keeping his father-in-law Jethro's sheep deep in the wilderness, near a mountain called Horeb. A former prince, walking behind sheep in the heat. An ordinary workday: no temple, no altar, no warning.
Then, out of the corner of his eye, a bush is on fire.

teach.h: IT BURNS, AND IS NOT CONSUMED.
teach.b: Bushes catch fire in the desert. What's strange is this, in the King James Bible: "the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed." It burns, and it doesn't burn up.
Moses says, "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." That small choice matters.

When the Lord saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him from the middle of the bush: "Moses, Moses." And Moses answers with the words Abraham and Jacob said before him: "Here am I." Then: don't come any closer.
"Put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." It's the same dirt he walked on yesterday with the sheep. What makes it holy is who is there.
God names himself, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob, and Moses hides his face, afraid to look. Christians have seen many things in this bush.

In Orthodox and Catholic tradition, a bush that holds fire without burning up became a picture of Mary, who carried God within her. In Ethiopian Orthodox churches, worshippers take off their shoes before they enter.
And the English poet Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote: "Earth's crammed with heaven, and every common bush afire with God; but only he who sees, takes off his shoes."

teach.h: THE PLACE WHEREON THOU STANDEST IS HOLY GROUND.
teach.b: The fire was there. Moses turned aside.

how: In Ethiopian Orthodox churches and some other Christian communities, worshippers remove their shoes before entering, and Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor an icon of the Unburnt Bush linked to Mary; Christians also read Exodus 3 as a call to notice God in ordinary places.

games.q: you're Moses, out with the sheep. off to the side, a bush is burning, and it isn't burning up. what do you do?

games.why: "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight." and when God saw that he turned aside, God called him by name.

practice: If you can, slip off your shoes and put your feet flat on the floor, the same floor you cross every day without noticing. For a minute, let it be holy ground.
If you pray, you can simply say, here am I; if you don't, just pay attention, the way Moses turned aside to see.

wordCard.voice: Seneh. Hebrew for the thorny bush that burned but was not consumed, where God called Moses by name and told him, holy ground.

orig.note: Hebrew: the word for this kind of thorny bush, used for the burning bush in Exodus 3.
